title: Second order effects: Redis fixed slow reads and created cache invalidation
story:
First-order thinking asks what the problem is and what solves it. Second-order thinking asks the only question that matters afterwards: and then what happens?

Here is the canonical case. Profile pages are slow because every view reaches the database and the database reaches disk. The fix is obvious and it works — put Redis in front, serve the reads from memory, and the latency falls by most of two orders of magnitude. The graph is unambiguous, the change is small, and the team is right to ship it.

Then the second order arrives, and notice that none of it is about read latency. When a user changes their avatar, how does the cache learn? Invalidation logic now has to exist in every service that writes a profile, which is a cross-cutting concern where there was none. Two writers race, and a stale pointer survives for as long as the entry lives. Memory fills, so keys are evicted on a policy nobody chose deliberately. And when the cache restarts cold, every request that used to be served from memory arrives at a database that has not carried that load since the day before.

That last one has a name and a literature. Vattani, Chierichetti and Lowenstein define a cache stampede as what happens when a frequently accessed item expires: many requests miss at once and all begin regenerating the same item, which severely limits database and web server performance. They note it is often called a cascading failure, because the concurrent recomputations lengthen each individual recomputation by bogging down the system, which in turn pulls even more requests into the stampede. The failure feeds itself, which is the property that distinguishes it from ordinary overload.

Their countermeasure is worth knowing because of its shape rather than its details. Let each process randomly request regeneration before the item expires, with the probability of volunteering rising as the entry approaches expiry. They give algorithms for such probabilistic early expirations which they show to be optimal, and which they report outperform the solutions used in real-world applications. It needs no coordination or locks, because every worker decides independently — the randomness is doing the work that a lock would otherwise do badly.

So the honest accounting is that Redis did not eliminate complexity. It traded read latency for cache coherence, memory management and a new failure mode at restart. That is usually a good trade. It is a trade regardless, and the second column only appears if somebody asks what happens next.

problem.name: Second-order accounting
problem.shape: A fix works on the metric it was chosen for, and the question is what it does to everything else.
tell: the benefit is measured and the costs are described as edge cases
a stateful component is being added to remove latency
the fix introduces a second copy of data that can disagree with the first
nobody has said what happens when the new component restarts empty
problem.move: Write down the first-order effect, then keep asking what happens next until the answers stop being about the original metric. For a cache specifically, name three things before shipping: who invalidates, what happens when two writers race, and what the database sees when the cache is cold.
problem.invariant: A fix does not remove complexity; it moves it. The second-order effects are in a different currency from the first-order benefit, which is why they are not noticed during the decision.
problem.breaks: Second-order reasoning generates more predictions than a team can act on, and most of them never happen. Treated as a veto it becomes an argument against every change, so it is a discipline for enumerating consequences and choosing which to mitigate, not a licence to refuse the trade.

cost.time: a design review before adding a stateful component, and mitigation work for failure modes that have not occurred yet
cost.space: the cache itself, plus whatever the stampede mitigation holds
cost.beats: shipping the first-order fix alone, which is faster and correct until the restart, and refusing the cache, which keeps one problem rather than exchanging it for three

worked.problem: Give an example of a common architecture fix where the second-order effect was worse than the original problem.
worked.reasoning:
Auto-scaling web servers in response to a slow database. The first-order reading is that queues are filling, so add capacity to drain them; the second-order reality is that the queues are filling because of the database, and each new instance opens its own connection pool. Capacity arrives as additional connections to the component that was already the constraint, so the fix converts a slow site into a dead one.

The structure is the same in the caching case, which is the one worth working through because the fix is genuinely good. Reads are slow, a cache serves them from memory, and latency falls by most of two orders of magnitude. Everything after that point is in a different currency. Invalidation has to be performed by every writer, which is a cross-cutting concern where there was none. Two writers racing leave a stale value for as long as the entry lives. Memory fills and eviction begins on a policy nobody chose. And a cold restart sends every previously cached read to a database that has not carried that load recently.

That last effect has a literature. A cache stampede is what happens when a frequently accessed item expires: many requests miss at once and all begin regenerating the same item, which severely limits database and web server performance. It is often called a cascading failure, because the concurrent recomputations lengthen each individual recomputation by bogging down the system, which in turn pulls even more requests in. That self-feeding property is what makes it different from ordinary overload — the load is being generated by the recovery.

The known countermeasure is worth knowing for its shape. Let each process randomly request regeneration before the item expires, with the probability of volunteering rising as the entry nears expiry. Algorithms for such probabilistic early expirations have been shown to be optimal and reported to outperform the solutions used in real-world applications, and they need no coordination or locks because every worker decides independently. The randomness does the job a lock would do badly.

What makes this hard in practice is not the reasoning but the asymmetry of the argument. The first-order benefit is measured, present and attributable. The second-order costs are hypothetical at the time of the decision, arrive later, and land on whoever is on call. So the person raising them is describing possibilities against somebody else's graph, which is why the enumeration has to happen as a habit rather than as a debate.

And the limitation should be stated, because second-order reasoning can be abused into a veto. Most of the predictions it generates never happen. The discipline is to enumerate the consequences and choose which to mitigate — not to conclude that because every fix has a second order, no fix should ship.

problem.practice: Take a cache in a system you work on and answer three questions in writing: who invalidates it, what two concurrent writers produce, and what the database sees in the first minute after the cache restarts empty. If any answer is 'nobody has checked', you have found the second-order effect.

beats.broke: A fix is judged by whether it solves the problem it was chosen for — and the problems it creates arrive later, in a different currency, owned by different people.
beats.fix: Ask what happens next, of the fix itself. A cache does not remove complexity; it exchanges read latency for invalidation, memory management and a cold-start failure mode.
beats.cost: The second-order effects are speculative when the decision is made and the first-order benefit is already measured, so the argument is permanently asymmetric and always sounds like obstruction.

interview.q: Give an example of a common architecture fix where the second-order effect was worse than the original problem.
interview.trap: Answering at the level of code rather than operational dynamics. The interesting failures are not bugs in the fix — the fix works exactly as designed, and the damage comes from what it does to the rest of the system.

takeaway: Every architectural fix is a mortgage: a cache buys read latency today and pays in invalidation, memory management and a cold-start stampede where the load is generated by the recovery — usually a good trade, but a trade only visible to someone who asks what happens next.
